Below is a single, consolidated 12-week program for your 30‑year‑old advanced-lifter client who is 20 weeks pregnant and OB‑cleared for moderate strength. It integrates the strength program, the higher-intensity Phase B (weeks 5–8) you requested, the pressing block that preserves her bench feel (without supine flat pressing), the pregnancy-safe core progression, cardio plan, and the nutrition guidance focused on maintaining lean mass. All programming respects contraindications: no supine after week 16, no maximal attempts, no contact sports; avoid Valsalva/true 1RMs; stop for any concerning symptoms.

Quick client summary / training principles
- Age / status: 30 / advanced lifter
- Pregnancy: 20 weeks (2nd trimester) — OB cleared for moderate strength
- Contraindications: no supine after week 16; no maximal attempts; no contact sports
- Overall frequency: 4 gym sessions/week (2 primary strength sessions — one heavy lower, one heavy upper; 1 posterior-chain/unilateral session; 1 conditioning/mobility/core session)

Frequency: 3 sessions/week baseline; combine steady-state, intervals, and pool-based options.

Phase A (weeks 1–4)

- 1 recovery/pool walk 20–30 min

Phase B (weeks 5–8)
- 1 steady-state 30–40 min
- 1 interval session 20–30 min (e.g., 60s RPE 6–7 / 120s easy × 6–8)
- 1 pool or recovery session 20–30 min
- Optional short 10–15 min post-strength finishers on 1–2 days

Phase C (weeks 9–12)
- 1 steady 20–30 min (reduce duration if fatigued)
- 1 low-volume interval 12–16 min (short intervals at RPE ≤7)
- 1 pool or brisk walk 20–30 min
- Prefer splitting cardio into 2 × 10–15 min bouts if needed

Nutrition plan summary (maintain lean mass; second-trimester targets)
- Calories: modest increase vs pre-pregnancy maintenance; typical +250–350 kcal/day in 2nd trimester. Adjust ± based on weight gain and appetite. Example target range ~2,450–3,200 kcal/day depending on baseline maintenance.
- Protein: target ~1.2–1.7 g/kg/day (practical ~1.4 g/kg). Example 70 kg → ~98 g/day. Emphasize 20–35 g protein per meal, include whey/protein shake post-workout if tolerated.
- Carbs: 40–55% of calories; prioritize whole grains, fruits, starchy veg; increase carbs around training.
- Fats: 25–35% calories; ensure DHA (200–300 mg/day) and unsaturated fats.
- Hydration: baseline ≥2.3 L/day plus more for workouts; include electrolytes as needed.
- Micronutrients: continue prenatal vitamin (folate, iron, vit D); monitor iron/ferritin; ensure iodine and DHA.
- Meal timing: protein evenly distributed across 3–4 meals + snacks; include pre- and post-workout snack.
- Practical sample day: Greek yogurt + oats + whey; cottage cheese + fruit snack; grilled chicken + quinoa + veg; pre/post workout rice cake + protein; salmon + sweet potato; cottage cheese snack.

Recovery & sleep
- Prioritize 7–9 hours sleep; naps if needed. At least 2 rest/active recovery days weekly. If training intensity rises (Phase B), increase protein post-workout, add a rest day if fatigue accumulates, and monitor pelvic-floor symptoms.

Monitoring, autoregulation & red flags
- Use RPE and symptom monitoring rather than strict HR zones.
- If RPE consistently >7.5 or pelvic pressure/leakage increases — reduce load/volume and consider pelvic health physio.
- Stop & contact OB for bleeding, contractions, decreased fetal movement, chest pain, dizziness, severe pain, or fluid leakage.

- Do NOT perform a true 1RM. Use submax tests, e.g.:
  - 2–3 top sets of 3 reps at RPE 7–7.5 on trap-bar deadlift and incline press (record weight & RPE).
  - Optionally perform a single heavy-but-not-maximal double or single at RPE ~7 for the “big lift” feeling.
  - Use velocity tracking or conservative 3–5RM estimates if desired; do not attempt estimated 1RM.

Coaching cues & practical notes
- Always warm up thoroughly and set up incline/seated positions properly for pressing.
- Cue gentle diaphragmatic inhale and controlled exhale on concentric; avoid breath-holding.
- Avoid prolonged supine; use incline bench (30–45°), seated machines, chest-supported tools, half-kneel and standing patterns.
- Be flexible: allow session substitutions for pool sessions or shorter bouts if nausea/fatigue present.
- Keep open contact with OB and refer to pelvic health physiotherapist for any PGP, urinary leakage, or diastasis concerns.

Below is a practical, pregnancy-safe nutrition plan tailored to an advanced lifter who’s 20 weeks pregnant and wants to maintain lean mass while supporting fetal growth. Overview and targets
- Energy: Aim for a modest caloric increase above pre-pregnancy needs. Typical guidance in the second trimester is +250–350 kcal/day.   - If pre-pregnancy maintenance was 2,200 kcal/day → target ~2,450–2,600 kcal/day.
  - If maintenance was 2,800 kcal/day → target ~3,000–3,200 kcal/day.
- Protein: 1.2–1.7 g/kg bodyweight per day (higher end if lean mass maintenance is priority and if tolerated). For example, a 70 kg client → 84–119 g protein/day; aim for ~1.4 g/kg as a practical target (~98 g/day).
- Carbohydrate: 40–55% of calories (emphasize complex carbs, whole grains, fruit, vegetables). Higher carbs around training sessions for performance and recovery.
- Fat: 25–35% of calories, with emphasis on unsaturated fats and omega-3 (DHA).
- Meal timing: Distribute protein fairly evenly (20–35 g per meal) across 3–4 meals + snacks. Have a carb + protein snack 30–90 min before training if tolerated, and a recovery snack within 1 hour after training.
- Hydration: At least 2.3 L/day fluid baseline plus more around training and in heat. Include electrolytes if heavy sweating.
- Micronutrients: Continue prenatal multi-vitamin. Prioritize iron, folate, iodine, vitamin D, calcium, and DHA. Work with OB/registered dietitian for labs (iron/ferritin) and supplementation as needed.

- Positional safety: No prolonged supine; prefer upright positions (treadmill walking, cycling, elliptical, recumbent bike only if comfortable but avoid supine recumbent positions), swimming, and water aerobics.
- Monitoring: Watch for uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, decreased fetal movement, dizziness, chest pain, or unusual shortness of breath — stop and contact OB if any occur.

- Swimming or pool walking: excellent for comfort, offloads joints and pelvic girdle strain; safe throughout pregnancy.
- Rowing: use cautiously — monitor posture and breath and avoid maximal efforts; preferable only if comfortable.

Short answer: No — do not test a true 1RM in week 12 (or at any point during pregnancy).

Why not
- Pregnancy contraindications include “no maximal attempts.” A 1RM test is a maximal effort that raises intra-abdominal pressure, often involves breath-holding (Valsalva), and can cause large transient spikes in blood pressure and heart rate. These responses may be uncomfortable or unsafe for the mother and could potentially stress the placenta or trigger uterine irritability.
- The OB clearance allowed “moderate strength.” Maximal testing contradicts that guidance and professional standards for exercise in pregnancy.
- Increased risk of pelvic floor overload, urinary leakage, or pelvic girdle pain with maximal loads, especially later in pregnancy.
- Balance and proprioception change as pregnancy advances; testing maximal single efforts increases injury risk.

What you can do instead (safe, practical “peak” testing to satisfy her desire to feel strong)
- Use submaximal strength tests and validated estimations, autoregulation methods, or structured performance checks that give meaningful feedback without true maximal attempts.

Options (pick one or combine):

1) RPE-based top-set test (recommended)
- After thorough warm-up, perform 1–2 top sets at an RPE target (e.g., RPE 7–7.5) for a low-rep set (2–4 reps) on a compound lift (safety-bar squat, trap-bar deadlift, incline press).
- Record weight, reps, and RPE. Repeatability gives a good measure of strength progress without maximal stress.
- Example: After warm-up, do 1 top set of trap-bar deadlift 3 reps at RPE 7. If last heavy week used 120 kg x 3 @ RPE 7, comparing week 12 performance vs baseline shows progress.

2) 3–5RM submax test with conservative RPE
- Test a 3RM or 5RM on a supported variation (safety-bar squat, trap-bar deadlift, incline press) but stop well short of failure (aim for RPE ≤7.5). Use experienced coaching, longer rests (2.5–3 min), and have spotters/safety boxes in place.
- Use conservative estimation formulas to estimate 1RM if desired, but interpret cautiously — avoid attempting the estimated 1RM.

3) Velocity or bar-speed monitoring (if available)
- Use a linear position transducer or phone app to measure bar velocity on moderate-heavy sets. Increased bar speed at the same load indicates strength/power gains without maximal loads.
- Protocol: 2–3 sets at a fixed submax load (e.g., 70% pre-pregnancy 1RM) and compare mean concentric velocity across weeks.

4) Rep-to-RPE benchmark (repeatable metric)
- Pick a benchmark set: e.g., incline press 5 x 5 at target RPE 7, or trap-bar deadlift 3 x 3 at RPE 7. Use the weight she can handle at target RPE as the comparison across time.
- Progress is judged by holding RPE constant while raising load or performing the same load for fewer RPE.

5) Functional strength tests (safe alternatives)
- Max loaded carry distance/time (suitcase/farmer carry) for a fixed weight — measures strength-endurance and translates to real-world function.
- Vertical push/pull tests with submax loads (e.g., 3–5RM incline press) as described above.

If she still really wants an estimated 1RM number
- You can estimate 1RM from a submax rep test (e.g., a well-performed 3–5RM) using validated formulas. But do not attempt the estimated 1RM — treat it only as a metric.
- Example: 3RM on incline press performed at RPE 7 can be plugged into an equation to estimate 1RM; use only for tracking.

How to structure a safe “peak week”/session (week 12)
- Keep volume lower and focus on high-quality technique and readiness.
- Example session:
  - Warm-up: 10–12 min aerobic + mobility + progressive warm-up sets
  - Heavy top sets (choose 1–2 lifts only): 2–3 work sets at RPE 7–7.5, 2–4 reps per set, 2–3 min rest
  - Bar-speed or submax 3RM test (optional): 3RM at RPE ≤7.5 on supported variation
  - 10–15 min accessory/core (as per pregnancy core plan)
  - Cool-down: mobility, diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic-floor relaxation
- Monitor symptoms closely; if any dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, contractions, bleeding, or pelvic pressure occurs, stop.

Coaching cues and safety during the session
- Clearly coach breathing—no Valsalva. Use a gentle exhale on concentric and controlled inhale on eccentric.
- Use safety equipment: spotters for incline press, safety pins/boxes on squats, and a coach near for balance assistance.
- Keep rest long (2.5–3.5 min) between heavy sets and hydrate between sets.
- Avoid testing multiple lifts to near-max in the same day. Limit to 1–2 lifts max.
- Prefer chest-supported, seated, safety-bar, or trap-bar variations for heavy work to reduce risk.

Documentation and psychological benefit
- Track weight, reps, and RPE across weeks. Showing consistent RPE at higher loads or same load at lower RPE demonstrates progress and gives the satisfaction of “peaking” without risking maximal attempts.
- If she wants the emotional experience of “hitting a big lift”, plan a well-coached heavy-but-submax top set (e.g., an RPE 7 single or double) that feels heavy and rewarding but is still within safety limits.

Bottom line
- True 1RM testing is contraindicated per “no maximal attempts” and is not advisable during pregnancy.
- Use submaximal, RPE/rep-based tests, velocity measures, or heavy-but-not-maximal top sets to provide measurable, satisfying performance feedback in week 12.

Peak‑week testing guidance (again)
- Do NOT test a true 1RM. Use submax top-sets (e.g., 3 reps at RPE 7–7.5) or 3–5RM at RPE ≤7.5 for tracking.

- If she wants a heavy feel, precede a top set with cluster sets or a heavy single at RPE 7 (not maximal), with long rests and safety measures in place.

Core program (integrated and progressive)
Frequency: 3 core mini-sessions per week (10–15 min), performed after sessions or on conditioning days.

Core Day A — Anti-extension (bird-dog, half-kneel dead-bug alternatives)
- Bird-dog: 3 × 8–10 each (progress to 3s holds / add band in later weeks)
- Tall-kneel/half-kneel anti-extension/shoulder band reach: 3 × 8–10 each
- Quadruped hip extensions: 3 × 10 each

Core Day B — Anti-rotation (Pallof variations)
- Pallof press: 3 × 8–12 each (standing → half-kneel → added resistance through weeks)
- Half-kneel landmine single-arm press (anti-rotation): 3 × 6–8 each
- Controlled standing chops: 3 × 10–12 each

Core Day C — Lateral chain & carries
- Side-lying clams / banded monster walks: 3 × 12–15
- Side-plank (knees → full → loaded): 2–3 × 20–30s each
- Farmer / suitcase carries (light-moderate): 3 × 30–45s

Progression: move from motor-control and low load (weeks 1–4) into higher-load anti-rotation and carries (weeks 5–8) and maintain/respect comfort in weeks 9–12. Watch for doming — regress if present.

Cardio plan (integrated)
Frequency: 3 sessions/week baseline; combine steady-state, intervals, and pool-based options.

Phase A (weeks 1–4)
- 1 steady-state 25–35 min (treadmill walk or bike)
- 1 interval session 20–25 min (e.g., 30s moderate / 90s easy × 8–10)
- 1 recovery/pool walk 20–30 min

Phase B (weeks 5–8)
- 1 steady-state 30–40 min
- 1 interval session 20–30 min (e.g., 60s RPE 6–7 / 120s easy × 6–8)
- 1 pool or recovery session 20–30 min
- Optional short 10–15 min post-strength finishers on 1–2 days

Phase C (weeks 9–12)
- 1 steady 20–30 min (reduce duration if fatigued)
- 1 low-volume interval 12–16 min (short intervals at RPE ≤7)
- 1 pool or brisk walk 20–30 min
- Prefer splitting cardio into 2 × 10–15 min bouts if needed

Nutrition plan summary (maintain lean mass; second-trimester targets)
- Calories: modest increase vs pre-pregnancy maintenance; typical +250–350 kcal/day in 2nd trimester. Adjust ± based on weight gain and appetite. Example target range ~2,450–3,200 kcal/day depending on baseline maintenance.
- Protein: target ~1.2–1.7 g/kg/day (practical ~1.4 g/kg). Example 70 kg → ~98 g/day. Emphasize 20–35 g protein per meal, include whey/protein shake post-workout if tolerated.
- Carbs: 40–55% of calories; prioritize whole grains, fruits, starchy veg; increase carbs around training.
- Fats: 25–35% calories; ensure DHA (200–300 mg/day) and unsaturated fats.
- Hydration: baseline ≥2.3 L/day plus more for workouts; include electrolytes as needed.
- Micronutrients: continue prenatal vitamin (folate, iron, vit D); monitor iron/ferritin; ensure iodine and DHA.
- Meal timing: protein evenly distributed across 3–4 meals + snacks; include pre- and post-workout snack.
- Practical sample day: Greek yogurt + oats + whey; cottage cheese + fruit snack; grilled chicken + quinoa + veg; pre/post workout rice cake + protein; salmon + sweet potato; cottage cheese snack.

Recovery & sleep
- Prioritize 7–9 hours sleep; naps if needed. At least 2 rest/active recovery days weekly. If training intensity rises (Phase B), increase protein post-workout, add a rest day if fatigue accumulates, and monitor pelvic-floor symptoms.

Monitoring, autoregulation & red flags
- Use RPE and symptom monitoring rather than strict HR zones.
- If RPE consistently >7.5 or pelvic pressure/leakage increases — reduce load/volume and consider pelvic health physio.
- Stop & contact OB for bleeding, contractions, decreased fetal movement, chest pain, dizziness, severe pain, or fluid leakage.

Week 12 testing alternative (recommended)
- Do NOT perform a true 1RM. Use submax tests, e.g.:
  - 2–3 top sets of 3 reps at RPE 7–7.5 on trap-bar deadlift and incline press (record weight & RPE).
  - Optionally perform a single heavy-but-not-maximal double or single at RPE ~7 for the “big lift” feeling.
  - Use velocity tracking or conservative 3–5RM estimates if desired; do not attempt estimated 1RM.

Coaching cues & practical notes
- Always warm up thoroughly and set up incline/seated positions properly for pressing.
- Cue gentle diaphragmatic inhale and controlled exhale on concentric; avoid breath-holding.
- Avoid prolonged supine; use incline bench (30–45°), seated machines, chest-supported tools, half-kneel and standing patterns.
- Be flexible: allow session substitutions for pool sessions or shorter bouts if nausea/fatigue present.
- Keep open contact with OB and refer to pelvic health physiotherapist for any PGP, urinary leakage, or diastasis concerns.
